# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

whys.g1: Access to cash when bills and salaries are due and money that is safe and insured are the two separate concerns I would sort these into, the names are plain, and Marcus's answer about paperwork and a better rate inside his own bank rightly stands alone because it fits neither.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

screens.why2: The question is plain, but Keel's belief line needs a second read because "cash waiting to be spent on their last cash decision" sounds as if the cash is being spent on the decision.
screens.why3: I built this because I needed it for my own startup's reserves, so I know exactly what it beats: lower yields from Mercury, Brex or Rho treasury and the work of managing it in-house.
screens.why4: The free-text box lets me give the advantage in my own words, and "Leave this out of the study" is a fitting escape if I do not want to test this belief.
screens.why5: "Higher yield" is kept, but the belief drops "without hiring for treasury", which is half of what I typed and part of why a founder would switch.
screens.instead: Keep the question, and write the belief as: "For most, it would have earned more on the cash from their raise, without hiring anyone to manage it, the last time they decided where that cash sits."

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today, Keel shows what it drafted from my answer and the belief it will test, so it is obvious why this is here.
screens.why2: Yield and treasury are everyday words to me, but "given them higher yield on their last cash decision" is clumsy and needs a second read, because a decision does not earn yield; the reserve does.
screens.why3: This is my own pitch and my own numbers (4.5-5% against about 3.5%), so I can judge straight away whether it is the advantage I claim.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but the claim I would most want beside them, more yield without switching banks or giving up safety, is missing, and the screen does not say why only the first row reaches the test.
screens.why5: "Higher yield on cash waiting to be spent" keeps my main claim, but the tested belief drops "without hiring for treasury" from my "Higher yield without hiring for treasury", and with it the point that the gain costs no extra work.
screens.instead: Belief to test: "For most, it would have earned more on the cash they last decided to leave sitting from their raise, without switching banks or hiring for treasury." Rows: "Higher yield on cash waiting to be spent" / "No need to switch banks" / "No need to hire for treasury".

screens.why1: After the fit and the advantage, asking what they must do to start is the obvious last piece of describing my solution, and it is new ground.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and 'setup' and 'extra steps' are how I already talk about my 'one-time setup that takes five minutes'.
screens.why3: I built the onboarding, so I know exactly what a finance lead has to do: connect the bank through Plaid and move the reserve.
screens.why4: The single escape chip fits, but the belief line picks only the reserve move and drops the Plaid link I typed, and 'Most would move' reads as a prediction rather than a step, so what I can check here is a little off.
screens.why5: My move-the-reserve step is kept in my words, but the Plaid link is gone from the belief and 'would move' turns my 'what they have to do' into a claim about how many will do it, which drifts a little.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? Any setup, extra steps or learning, up to 25 words; then show each step I typed as its own belief to confirm: 'Link the company bank account through Plaid' and 'Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury'.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they must do to start, Keel plays back the setup steps and the one belief to test, so it is obvious why it sits here as the last of the four solution checks.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are all everyday words to me and to a startup finance lead, and each row reads clean on first pass.
screens.why3: These are the exact steps I walk my own customers through and did for my own startup's cash, so I can judge them directly from what I know.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but the list skips the steps that really take effort, such as agreeing the first small amount to move and the custody or advisory onboarding, and it assumes the reserve sits in the bank's treasury when some startups hold it in plain checking.
screens.why5: The steps are mine, but 'Most would move the long-term reserve' drifts from my pitch of starting small and growing the position over time, because it tests moving the whole reserve as if that were the first step.
screens.instead: Rows: Link the company bank account through Plaid; Move part of the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury or checking. Belief: Most would move part of their long-term reserve out of where it sits today.

screens.why1: Right after I checked what they must do to start, it is obvious why Keel asks me to pick the one step to test, and moving the reserve is the step the idea stands on.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are the words I and every finance lead at a Mercury or Brex startup use, and the belief and the 1-in-3 bar read clean the first time.
screens.why3: I built this because of my own startup's cash, so I know linking takes minutes and that moving the reserve is where people balk, as my HN thread showed.
screens.why4: Both options are mine and distinct and the real sticking point is there, but the list omits the first small test transfer I told people to start with, which is the step many would actually take.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to offer a pilot to the people who answer.
screens.why2: The words are short and plain, but 'pilot' for a 0.25% fee on treasury balances takes a second read, because a treasury product would more naturally start with a small first deposit than a pilot.
screens.why3: Whether I would take early users is my own decision, and I already tell people to start small and grow their position.
screens.why4: The record shows only a Continue action and no options, rows or chips to judge.
screens.why5: It adds nothing to my idea, and the hint says it leaves people's answers unchanged, so what I typed still means the same.
screens.instead: Offer people who answer the chance to try it early with a small part of their reserve? Optional, and nothing here changes their answers.

screens.why1: Choosing who puts the questions to people is an obvious last decision before the study goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint's 'runs on its own AI' and 'Keel's credits' take a second read, and the typed answer's 'lock and record the face' is not how I would describe anything in my work.
screens.why3: How my study reaches founders and finance leads is my own call, and I know whether I would pay for an interviewer.
screens.why4: The only choice recorded is a preselected face, so I cannot tell what the alternatives are or how the AI interviewer differs from people reading and tapping, and the hint suggests that the choice may already be limited on this account.

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, the next obvious thing to settle is who receives the link, and this comes last before sending.
screens.why2: Named people, a Contacts search and one open link in a group are all clear to me on first reading, and 'link' is an everyday word for a founder.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to: batchmates and founders and finance leads I can name, or a YC or founder group where I could post.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but 'People I found with Keel' also ends in individual links I send myself, so it overlaps a little with the first option, and a mix of routes is not offered.
screens.why5: The screen makes no claim about my idea or roles, and my choice of people I know by name is kept as I picked it.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check whether my company's banking setup fits before asking anything else.
screens.why2: Mercury and Brex are names I deal with every day, so I can answer at once, though "or similar" is a little loose.
screens.why3: I run the company's bank accounts, so I know exactly where we bank.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct and in my words, but "or similar" leaves a company with a traditional bank or several banks unsure which to pick.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment wording about banking with Mercury, Brex or similar and tells me nothing about a product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that I can hear once and answer, and the comma after Mercury says naturally.
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its operating cash at a fintech banking platform like Mercury or Brex? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: After the banking question, a question about my cash is plausible, but it jumps to a loaded idea of idle cash, and a yes then leads to my last cash decision, which is a different subject.
screens.why2: I can answer quickly, but I'd have to stop and work out what 'idle' means, since our cash sits in a treasury or sweep account at about 3.2%, and nobody I work with says 'see your raised cash'.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our cash is every day, but whether part of it counts as idle is a judgement call, so my yes or no would be partly a guess at what they mean.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct, but the true answer of 'some in operating, the rest earning' has no home, and the 'one particular cash decision' chip doesn't fit a question about idle cash, with 'I'd rather not say' as a second escape.
screens.why5: No product leaks, but 'sit idle' sounds like someone's pitch that my cash should be working harder, not a neutral word for how I hold it.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question with 'Yes or no' and I can answer after one hearing, though 'raised cash' is slightly stiff.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you decide or review where the cash from your raise is held? Yes / No

screens.why1: After two questions about where we bank and whether cash sat idle, Part 2 opens by showing me the idea, so it is obvious why this card is here.
screens.why2: Plaid, custodian and treasury account are plain to me, but "repaid soon, with moving rates" is not how I talk about short-duration floating-rate government bonds, and "long-term reserve" sits oddly beside it, so I need a second read.
screens.why3: Moving reserve cash, liquidity timing and yield are decisions I handle myself, so I can weigh this card from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The card shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: An idea card is meant to show me the product, but the wording has drifted: "holds them" has no clear referent, a full stop is missing, and the last line runs together as "target 4.5 to 5 percent, return cash", repeating the one-to-two-day claim like a pasted fragment.
screens.why6: It can be said with no parenthesis or slash, but the bond sentence is a mouthful, the missing full stop runs the custodian line into "The people building it", and the broken last line says the liquidity claim a second time.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus. You link a treasury account to your existing bank through Plaid, and it holds your reserve cash in short-term, floating-rate government bonds, held by a regulated custodian in your company's name. The people building it believe it would target 4.5 to 5 percent and return cash to checking in one to two business days.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, it makes sense to ask whether a two-day wait on my cash would work for me, because that wait is what I'd weigh first.
screens.why2: "Cash decision" isn't how I'd put it, and "waited two days for your cash" takes a second read to work out that it means money taking two days to reach my operating account.
screens.why3: I know when bills and payroll hit, so I can judge a two-day wait, but my last decision may have been to leave the cash where it was, which leaves me guessing about a wait that never came up.
screens.why4: The range and "I can't tell" fit, but "Only sometimes" is odd for one past decision and "Yes, easily" and "Yes, mostly" sit close together.
screens.why5: Only the name Palus appears, as part of the card shown on purpose, and the two-day wait reads as a plain condition with no product pitch or role labels leaking through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after hearing them once, and the escape comes last, though "Yes, easily" and "Yes, mostly" sound close aloud.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you moved cash to cover payroll or a bill. Could that money have taken two days to arrive, or not? Yes, easily; Yes, with some juggling; No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the two-day wait question, asking whether this thing would have helped my last cash decision is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Made it go better" is vague because "it" points back to a cash decision anchored on the previous screen, and I had to reread to work out that it means where we parked the cash and what we earned.
screens.why3: I made that decision and know what mattered, which for me was operational burden over yield, so I can say whether it would have changed anything.
screens.why4: The four options are distinct, cover my likely answer of no difference as well as worse, and "I can't tell" fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The name Palus is part of the idea card shown on purpose, and nothing else from the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is short with an easy list to hold, but heard once the "it" has nothing to attach to unless I remember the earlier anchor, so the stem doesn't quite stand on its own.
screens.instead: Would Palus have made your last cash decision go better for you, or not? A lot better; A little better; No difference; or Worse. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After I said the idea wouldn't change much, it makes sense to ask what would actually help before closing out.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but "keeping money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it" is a long, stiff way to say managing our raise cash, and I'd just say treasury or idle cash.
screens.why3: This is my job, and I can say what would help: less operational hassle and fewer accounts to manage, since I care about that more than squeezing out extra yield.
screens.why4: There are no options on this screen, only a box to type in.
screens.why5: The meaning holds and Palus was already introduced on the card, but the wording reads like a pasted job statement rather than anything said to me, and "wouldn't make much difference" is a paraphrase of my answer I can't be sure I'd own.
screens.why6: It is one question and can be said, but the second sentence runs to about 20 words with a mouthful in the middle, plus a tacked-on "if anything", so I'd want to hear it twice.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't make much difference on your last cash decision. What would make managing your raise cash better for you, if anything?

screens.why1: Whether I'd actually move the money is the right thing to ask about Palus, but it comes back to 3 of 3 after a "One more thing" question had already felt like the wrap-up, and after I'd said Palus wouldn't change much.
screens.why2: "Bank's treasury" is plain to me because that's how Mercury and Brex talk, but I'd say "our runway cash" or "what's in treasury", not "long-term reserve", so I had to think about which money it meant.
screens.why3: Where our cash sits and whether I'd move it is my call to make or recommend, so I can answer this from how I run things today.
screens.why4: My true answer, "No", is there, but "Probably not" and "No" sit close together, there's no softer yes, the only condition offered is speed when my real worry is the extra operational work, and the "i" is lowercase.
screens.why5: It says plainly what Palus would ask of me, and the name is expected after the idea card, so nothing leaks that shouldn't.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is short, with one question and four options I can hold, and it ends with a single escape, though the "Only if" option is longer than the rest.
screens.instead: Palus means moving your runway cash out of your bank's treasury account. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Only if I could get the cash back quickly; Only if it added no extra work; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move the reserve, so asking what makes it too much trouble is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are how I talk about our cash, and I can take the question in on one read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would be a pain, because I run these accounts and the operational burden is what I weigh over yield.
screens.why4: It is only a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It assumes my no meant too much trouble, when the reason could be safety or trust, so it puts a reason in my mouth, though no product terms leak.
screens.why6: It is one short question of under 20 words with no symbols, and it says well and is easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: What makes you not want to move the long-term reserve out of your bank's treasury?
